lines.text: Do you know the first plane to fly faster than sound was shaped like a bullet?
This is the real Bell X-1, laser scanned by the Smithsonian. Its body copies a fifty-calibre machine gun bullet.
Bullets were already known to stay stable faster than sound. No plane had ever flown that fast.
Sound is a pressure wave. Near the ground, it travels about three hundred and forty metres every second.
As a plane gets close to that speed, its own pressure waves can't get out of the way. They pile up into a shock wave.
Shock waves made normal elevators useless. So on the X-1, the whole tail could tilt, to keep control.
It didn't take off from the ground. A B-29 bomber carried it up, and dropped it.
Then four rocket chambers lit up, burning alcohol and liquid oxygen.
October fourteenth, nineteen forty-seven. Thirteen point seven kilometres up, where the air is colder, and sound is slower.
Mach one point zero five. The X-1 passed its own sound, and the shock wave swept back into a cone.
On the ground, people heard nothing. Until the cone swept over them. Boom.
Today, the real X-1 is on display at the Smithsonian, in Washington.
Speed comes from smart engineering. Orbi Transfer splits big files into parts.
It uploads three parts at a time, and downloads four at once. Files up to twenty gigabytes.
